title: Ontario population modeling
text:
Original course project
In January–May 2023, I collaborated in a five-member Introduction to Modelling team at McMaster University. My contributions included assumptions, variable organization, and interpretation of Ontario population trends.

title: Ontario population modeling
text:
Reconstructed R analysis
In November 2026, I reconstructed the analysis using Statistics Canada’s July 1 population estimates: 52 annual observations from 1971–2022. The original report was not recovered, so the estimates, validation results, and figure on this page belong to the reconstruction.
The model uses total population. Births, deaths, and migration provide demographic context; the fitted model does not estimate their separate effects.
I compared two logistic estimation approaches—numerical differentiation and nonlinear least squares—with linear and exponential trends. Models were fitted to 1971–2012 and evaluated on 2013–2022, a fixed ten-year holdout.

Observed Ontario population and four forecasts for 2013–2022, estimated only from data through 2012.



The nonlinear logistic model fitted the full historical sample most closely, but the derivative-based model performed best on the holdout. This distinction showed why historical goodness of fit alone was insufficient for choosing a forecasting method.

title: Ontario population modeling
text:
Model limits
Results were sensitive to the fitting window, and the logistic asymptote should not be interpreted as Ontario’s physical population capacity. Residual dependence and underprediction of later population growth further limited the model’s usefulness as a current forecast. One ten-year holdout did not establish that a method would remain best in other periods.
The reconstruction used revised historical estimates downloaded in November 2026. It was a retrospective modeling exercise rather than a forecast made with the data vintage available in 2023.
Data source: Statistics Canada, Table 17-10-0005-01, Ontario, all ages, total gender, July 1 population. Numerical results were checked against the reconstructed report and exported R tables.

I earned my Honours B.Sc. in Mathematics & Statistics, with a minor in Economics, at McMaster University. That training shaped the way I approach a question: examine the assumptions, organize the evidence, and explain what the analysis can support.
At Boston University, I’m building on that foundation through coursework in financial analytics, quantitative methods for finance, generative AI, and big data and cloud analytics. My academic projects span corporate filings, employer branding, financial statements, and population modeling.
My career goal is to contribute to financial or business analytics work where careful analysis and clear communication matter. I’m particularly interested in applying AI to financial information while keeping results traceable to their sources.

SEC 10-K extraction and retrieval

Applied Generative AI for Business Analytics · Group project · January–May 2026

Question: How can a large collection of corporate filings be organized for relevant, traceable financial research?
I worked on processing 7,754 SEC 10-K filings from 2024 across seven SIC industry groups. The workflow included text cleaning, section extraction, sentence segmentation, and metadata organization.
The project extracted Item 1A (Risk Factors) and Item 7 (Management’s Discussion and Analysis). A retrieval pipeline used structured metadata and section filters to support focused searches and source traceability.
This work connected document processing with the information needs of financial and risk analysis.

Ontario population growth modeling

Introduction to Modelling · Group project · January–May 2023

Question: How can a mathematical model help interpret long-term population trends in Ontario?
I collaborated in a five-member team developing a logistic population growth model. My contributions included model assumptions, variable organization, and interpretation of demographic trends.
In November 2026, I reconstructed the R analysis using 52 annual Statistics Canada observations (1971–2022) and fitted logistic models with numerical differentiation and nonlinear least squares. Four models were compared on a ten-year holdout (2013–2022): derivative-based logistic achieved 0.65% MAPE, versus 0.90% for a linear trend.
These estimates belong to the 2026 reconstruction. The original 2023 project contributions remain distinct.

title: Hackathon case study
text:
The business question
How could Booz Allen Hamilton improve its recruitment information and employment offering for early-career talent? We examined its job postings and employee reviews, then used Accenture and Capgemini as comparison firms to understand which themes stood out.

title: Hackathon case study
text:
My contribution
I cleaned 505 job postings and 1,245 employee reviews, removing HTML artifacts, standardizing missing values, and checking duplicate IDs and rating consistency. I contributed to comparing employer promises with employee feedback and developing recommendations for clearer recruitment information and project-transition support.
The findings and recommendations below describe the team’s work.

title: Hackathon case study
text:
Evidence and analytical approach
The sample contained 217 Booz Allen postings, 157 Accenture postings, and 131 Capgemini postings, with 415 employee reviews per company. We aggregated postings and reviews separately by company and theme, preserving each source’s denominator rather than treating them as matched employee–vacancy pairs.




Original project figure: 217 Booz Allen, 131 Capgemini, and 157 Accenture job postings; 415 employee reviews for each employer.



The team’s text-label framework covered employer promises, working conditions, and nine dimensions of employee sentiment. We first established a posting-only baseline, then examined how employee reviews supported or qualified that picture.

title: Hackathon case study
text:
What the comparison showed

Booz Allen Hamilton: advertised learning and benefits, together with positive work-life signals in reviews, coexisted with employee concerns about project stability and management. The practical question was how clearly candidates understood project transitions and available support.
Accenture: career-growth messaging was considered alongside review concerns about advancement, pay, and workload. We treated this as potential tension within the sample, rather than proof of an experience shared by every employee.
Capgemini: flexibility and work-life signals showed some alignment, while conclusions about career growth and pay changed with the review-title mix. A sensitivity check excluded I-CAP/onboarding-related titles, leaving 172 reviews under the broader exclusion rule; it did not establish that those excluded reviews were invalid.

title: Hackathon case study
text:
Recommendations
Clearer, role-specific recruitment information. Explain the actual work arrangement, requirements, benefits eligibility, and application process. Feature strengths that can be verified for the specific role. Proposed measures included posting completeness and qualified application completion.
Career and project-transition transparency. Explain pay and promotion criteria, project dependencies, reassignment support, and transferable skills. These were proposed improvements, rather than claims about an existing company policy. Suggested measures included candidate comprehension, expectation match, and time to reassignment.

title: Hackathon case study
text:
Validation and interpretation
The presentation included a 30-passage check spanning 270 dimension-level label comparisons. Its reference labels were assistant-assigned, so the reported agreement was a preliminary diagnostic rather than independently human-validated model accuracy.
The data were historical and the companies differed in role, location, date, and review composition. Employee accounts were not verified descriptions of every role, and the files contained no hiring or retention outcomes. Our recommendations therefore included future measurement rather than claims of proven recruitment uplift.
